nodes.name: Interacting Langevin diffusion (ensemble Kalman sampler dynamics)
nodes.statement: In \cite{sr:GIHLS19}, the authors propose to evolve an interacting set of particles $U = \{u^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^J$ according to the following system of stochastic differential equations (SDEs): \begin{equation} \dot{u}^{(j)} = -C(U)\nabla \Psi_R(u^{(j)}) + \sqrt{2C(U)} \dot{\bf W}^{(j)}, \end{equation} where $\Psi_R$ is a suitable potential and the ${\bf W}^{(j)}$ are a collection of i.i.d.~standard Brownian motions in the state space $\mathbb{R}^d$, aiming at approximating the posterior $\pi^\ast \propto \exp(-\Psi_R)$ in the long-time limit.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Particles $u^{(j)}$ evolve by preconditioned Langevin SDEs with covariance $C(U)$ to sample $\pi^\ast\propto e^{-\Psi_R}$.

nodes.name: Empirical covariance and sample mean
nodes.statement: The matrix $C(U)$ is chosen to be the empirical covariance between particles, \begin{equation} C(U) = \frac{1}{J} \sum_{k=1}^J (u^{(k)}-\bar{u})(u^{(k)}-\bar u)^{\rm T} \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, \end{equation} where $\bar u$ denotes the sample mean \begin{equation} \bar u = \frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^J u^{(j)}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: $C(U)$ is the empirical particle covariance about the sample mean $\bar u$.

nodes.name: Ensemble size exceeds dimension
nodes.statement: We require $J>d$ in order for $C(U)$ to have full rank generically.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Validity for small ensembles
nodes.statement: But we also note that (\ref{eq:IPS1}) is valid even for $J\le d$ in which case the dynamics is restricted to a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^d$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

abla \cdot \left( ho\, \mathcal{C} (ho)
abla \Psi_R + ho \,\mathcal{C}(ho)
abla \ln ho ight) =

nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Formal $J\to\infty$ limit gives a mean-field SDE whose marginal density solves a nonlinear Fokker--Planck gradient flow.

nodes.name: Macroscopic mean, covariance and energy functional
nodes.statement: Here we have defined the macroscopic mean and covariance \begin{equation} m(\rho) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} u \rho(u) \,{\rm d}u, \qquad \mathcal{C}(\rho) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} (u-m(\rho))(u-m(\rho))^{\rm T} \rho(u)\, {\rm d}u \end{equation} and the energy functional \begin{equation} E(\rho) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \rho(u) \left(\Psi_R(u) + \ln\rho(u)\right) {\rm d}u. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Mean $m(\rho)$, covariance $\mathcal{C}(\rho)$ of a density, and free energy $E(\rho)$.

nodes.name: Product target measure
nodes.statement: Our first step is to check whether the product measure \begin{equation} \pi(U) = \prod_{j=1}^J \pi^\ast(u^{(j)}) \end{equation} is invariant under (\ref{eq:IPS1}).
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system

nodes.name: Block-diagonal preconditioner $S(U)$
nodes.statement: We now rewrite (\ref{eq:IPS1}) in the form \begin{equation} \dot{U} = S(U)\nabla \ln \pi(U) + \sqrt{2S(U)}\dot{\bf W}, \end{equation} where $S(U) \in \mathbb{R}^{D\times D}$, $D = dJ$, is a block diagonal matrix with $J$ $d\times d$ entries $C(U)$ and ${\bf W}$ denotes standard $D$-dimensional Brownian motion.
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system
nodes.statement_short: Stacked form of the particle system with block-diagonal $S(U)=\mathrm{diag}(C(U),\dots,C(U))$ on $\mathbb{R}^{dJ}$.

nodes.statement: From \eqref{eq:FPE0} we see immediately that $\nabla \cdot (\pi \nabla \cdot S) = 0$ is a necessary condition for the invariance of $\pi$.

nodes.label: lemma1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation: divergence identities for rank-one products, applied to $C(U)=\frac1J\sum u u^T-\bar u\bar u^T$.

nodes.name: One-dimensional Gaussian target
nodes.statement: Let us consider a one-dimensional Gaussian target measure ($d=1$) with variance $b^2$, i.e. the potential is given by $\Psi_R(u) = u^2/(2b^2)$. Under the approximating assumptions that the equilibrium density associated to \eqref{eq:IPS1} is a product of $J$ Gaussians with variance $\sigma^2$, and that the covariance at equilibrium can be well-approximated by the state-independent stationary covariance (mean-field assumption), one can derive the relation \begin{equation} \sigma^2 \approx \frac{J-2}{J} b^2, \end{equation} which we numerically verified for $J=4$. Note that $\sigma^2 < b^2$, i.e. the dynamics \eqref{eq:IPS1} systematically underestimates the posterior variance. Since $ \sigma^2 \xrightarrow{J \rightarrow \infty} b^2$, this error vanishes in the large-particle regime, in agreement with the results in \cite{sr:GIHLS19}.
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system
nodes.statement_short: For a 1D Gaussian target the uncorrected dynamics has variance $\approx\frac{J-2}{J}b^2$, underestimating the posterior variance.

nodes.name: Corrected ensemble Kalman sampler dynamics
nodes.statement: More specifically, Lemma \ref{lemma1} implies that the corrected dynamics \begin{equation} \dot{u}^{(j)} = -C(U)\nabla \Psi_R(u^{(j)}) + \frac{d+1}{J} (u^{(j)}-\bar u) + \sqrt{2C(U)} \dot{\bf W}^{(j)}, \end{equation} or, written more compactly \begin{equation} \dot{U} = S(U)\nabla \ln \pi(U) + \frac{d+1}{J}(U-\bar U) + \sqrt{2S(U)}\dot{\bf W}, \end{equation} not only samples from the correct target density (\ref{eq:TPDF}) but also gives rise to a gradient flow structure for the time evolution of the joint density $\mu$ over all particles at time $t \ge 0$.
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system
conclusions: not only samples from the correct target density (\ref{eq:TPDF})
gives rise to a gradient flow structure for the time evolution of the joint density $\mu$ over all particles at time $t \ge 0$
nodes.statement_short: Adding the drift $\frac{d+1}{J}(u^{(j)}-\bar u)$ makes the product posterior invariant and yields a gradient-flow structure.

nodes.name: Gradient-flow Fokker--Planck equation for corrected system
nodes.statement:
The Fokker--Planck equation associated to the time evolution of the joint density $\mu$ under the corrected interacting particle formulation (ef{eq:IPS2c}) is of the form  egin{equation} \partial_t \mu = 
abla \cdot \left( \mu\, S 
abla \left\{ \ln \mu - \ln \pi ight\} ight) = 
abla \cdot \left( \mu \,S 
abla  rac{\delta V}{\delta \mu}ight), \end{equation} where the energy functional $V$ is the Kullback--Leibler divergence between $\mu$ and $\pi$, given by  egin{equation} V(\mu) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^D} \mu(U) \{\ln \mu (U) - \ln \pi(U) \} \, {m d}U. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system
assumptions: under the corrected interacting particle formulation (\ref{eq:IPS2c})
nodes.statement_short: The corrected system's Fokker--Planck equation is a $S$-preconditioned gradient flow of the KL divergence to $\pi$.
nodes.label: lemma2

nodes.name: Kalman--Wasserstein gradient flow for finite ensembles
nodes.statement: Hence the Kalman--Wasserstein gradient flow structure also carries over to the corrected finite-size particle system (\ref{eq:IPS2c}).

conclusions: the Kalman--Wasserstein gradient flow structure also carries over to the corrected finite-size particle system (\ref{eq:IPS2c})

nodes.name: Possible loss of positive definiteness
nodes.statement: However, it cannot be guaranteed that $C(U)$ remains strictly positive definite for all times, in general, even under the condition $J>d$.
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system

nodes.name: Regularised covariance
nodes.statement: This suggests a regularisation of the form \begin{equation} C_{\alpha}(U) = \alpha C_0 + (1-\alpha)C(U), \end{equation} where $C_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ is a fixed symmetric strictly positive definite matrix and $\alpha \in (0,1)$ is a parameter.
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system

nodes.name: Exponential convergence of the regularised corrected system
nodes.statement: Under the Bakry--{\'E}mery condition \cite{sr:P14} stated in Proposition 2 of \cite{sr:GIHLS19} one can then also establish exponential convergence to the equilibrium measure for the finite-size particle system (\ref{eq:IPS1c}) with $C(U)$ replaced by $C_\alpha(U)$ and the correction term by $(1-\alpha) (d+1) (u^{(j)}-\bar u)/J$.
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system
assumptions: Under the Bakry--{\'E}mery condition \cite{sr:P14} stated in Proposition 2 of \cite{sr:GIHLS19}
with $C(U)$ replaced by $C_\alpha(U)$ and the correction term by $(1-\alpha) (d+1) (u^{(j)}-\bar u)/J$
conclusions: one can then also establish exponential convergence to the equilibrium measure for the finite-size particle system (\ref{eq:IPS1c})
nodes.statement_short: Under Bakry--Emery, the regularised corrected particle system converges exponentially fast to the product posterior.

nodes.name: Justification of exponential convergence
nodes.statement: This follows from standard arguments for the classical Fokker--Planck equation \cite{sr:P14}. See also Proposition 2 of \cite{sr:GIHLS19}.
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system
nodes.statement_short: Appeal to standard Bakry--Emery arguments for the classical Fokker--Planck equation.

nodes.name: Holley--Stroock relaxation of convexity
nodes.statement: Let us also mention that the convexity requirement on $\Psi_R$ can be relaxed by a perturbation argument due to Holley–-Stroock \cite{sr:P14}.
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system

nodes.name: Avoiding the correction term
nodes.statement: The need for a correction term in (\ref{eq:IPS1}) can be avoided by ensuring that the $j$th block entry $C(U)$ in $S(U)$ does not depend on the $j$th particle position $u^{(j)}$.
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system

nodes.statement_short: Leave-one-out covariances $C_{[j]}$ and means $\bar u_{[j]}$ define a particle SDE needing no correction term.

nodes.name: Computational cost of leave-one-out formulation
nodes.statement: However, while the reformulation (\ref{eq:IPS3}) is appealing, its computational implementation is more demanding due to the need for computing $J$ different covariance matrices and their square roots.
nodes.section: 2 Properties of the finite-size particle system

nodes.name: Leave-one-out formulation as basis for gradient-free samplers
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if the destabilising effect of the correction term in (\ref{eq:IPS1c}) leads to numerical difficulties under small or moderate particle sizes, then (\ref{eq:IPS3}) could be taken as a starting point for formulating gradient-free formulations in the spirit of the ensemble Kalman sampler (EKS) as proposed in \cite{sr:GIHLS19}.
